options.text: Earth’s largest waterfall is underwater between Greenland and Iceland. Cold Nordic water sinks beneath warmer water and spills down a drop in the seabed.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: In 1941, HMS Hood sank here during a 16-minute battle with the Bismarck. Only three of the 1,415 people aboard survived.
options.label: Royal Navy

options.text: Instruments between Greenland and Iceland have measured pulses of deep water sweeping through roughly every five days. Even the current at the bottom of this strait has a rhythm.
options.label: Journal of Physical Oceanography

options.text: Sea ice can drift south through the Denmark Strait from the Arctic. It hugs the Greenland side as the East Greenland Current carries it past Iceland.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The vaquita lives only in the northern Gulf of California. No other whale, dolphin, or porpoise has such a small range.
options.label: NOAA Fisheries

options.text: More than 3½ km beneath the gulf, a research robot filmed what looks like an upside-down waterfall. Hot vent fluid rises and spills around a rock overhang.
options.label: MBARI expedition footage

options.text: Some islands here were once joined to the mainland by land bridges. On others, wildlife had to arrive by sea or air.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Gulf of California is opening along a plate boundary. Baja California rides with the Pacific Plate while most of mainland Mexico stays on the North American Plate.
options.label: pubs.usgs.gov

options.text: There is a pool with its own surface beneath the sea at East Flower Garden Bank. Water seeping out of a salt dome is so salty and dense that it settles into a hollow under ordinary seawater.
options.label: flowergarden.noaa.gov

options.text: Some coral reefs in the northwestern gulf sit on hills pushed up by salt. Deep deposits rose under the seabed, lifting the tops of the banks into sunlit water.
options.label: flowergarden.noaa.gov

options.text: Rings of warm Caribbean water can break away from the Loop Current. They travel west across the gulf long after the main current has turned towards Florida.
options.label: flowergarden.noaa.gov

options.text: Water can enter the gulf from the Caribbean, swing far north and leave again beside Florida. This Loop Current feeds the Gulf Stream before it heads across the Atlantic.
options.label: oceanservice.noaa.gov

options.text: A Greek trading ship survived intact more than two kilometres beneath the Black Sea. The deep water lacks oxygen, allowing even ancient wood to survive.
options.label: University of Southampton

options.text: The sea has a second, ancient coastline. Researchers have mapped prehistoric shorelines about 150 metres beneath today’s surface.
options.label: University of Rhode Island

options.text: The Black Sea can look turquoise from space. Blooms of microscopic plankton covered in chalky plates can turn the surface milky blue.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Black Sea trades water with the Mediterranean in two directions through one strait. Fresher Black Sea water flows out near the surface of the Bosporus while saltier water flows in underneath.
options.label: whoi.edu

options.text: The Aral Sea once acted like a giant radiator for the surrounding land. As it shrank, nearby winters grew colder and summers grew hotter and drier.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: As the water grew too salty for familiar catches, fisheries turned to an introduced flatfish. Flounder could survive where many of the old commercial species could no longer live.
options.label: documents.worldbank.org

options.text: The Aral Sea's shoreline retreated in part because cotton was being grown far upstream. Water diverted to irrigate fields never finished the journey to the lake.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In 2014 the entire eastern lobe of the South Aral Sea dried up. Within a human lifetime, a basin that helped make this the fourth-largest lake on Earth had become land.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Vjetrenica Cave breathes with the seasons. Stand at its mouth in warm weather and air blows out toward you. In cold weather it flows the other way.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Look closely at the region’s medieval gravestones, called stećci, and you can find people dancing, hunting, and jousting.
options.label: UNESCO nomination evaluation

options.text: A medieval Jewish manuscript survived World War II in Bosnia. Sarajevo’s National Museum recounts that it was sheltered in a mosque in a mountain village, then returned to the museum.
options.label: National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina

options.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina reaches the Adriatic through a narrow strip at Neum. Until Croatia bridged the bay in 2022, the main coastal drive to Dubrovnik crossed Bosnia twice.
options.label: regions-and-cities.ec.europa.eu

options.text: At Lepenski Vir on the Danube, prehistoric sculptors carved monumental stone faces with fishlike features. You can still see the sculptures today.
options.label: National Museum of Serbia

options.text: On the Serbian bank of the Danube, engineers moved a Roman inscription and a piece of the road it commemorates uphill so a hydroelectric dam would not drown them.
options.label: Tourism Organisation of Serbia

options.text: At a Serbian family’s slava, the celebration of its patron saint, a special loaf is marked with a cross, sprinkled with wine, and broken four ways.
options.label: Tourism Organisation of Serbia

options.text: On the Serbian–Romanian border the Danube cuts right across the Carpathian mountain chain. The result is the Iron Gates, a string of gorges through the mountains.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Some sand in Namibia’s coastal dunes travelled thousands of kilometres to get there, carried first by a river, then by ocean currents, and finally by wind.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Fog is the main source of water for life in the Namib Sand Sea. That bank of fog rolling in from the Atlantic helps sustain animals in the dunes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Follow the narrow finger in Namibia’s northeast and you reach the Zambezi. An 1890 agreement between Britain and Germany drew that corridor to give the colony access to the river.
options.label: International Boundary Study

options.text: Namibia's Fish River can shrink to a trickle in the dry season. Over geological time it has carved a canyon as much as 550 metres deep into the southern plateau.
options.label: mme.gov.na

options.text: Some of the black bitumen used to embalm Egyptian mummies came from the Dead Sea. Researchers have traced the material in mummy samples back to its source.
options.label: Archaeometry

options.text: The Jordan River flows into the Dead Sea, but no river flows out. Water escapes by evaporation, leaving salts behind.
options.label: ESA

options.text: The neat rectangles visible from space at the southern end of the Dead Sea are evaporation ponds for harvesting minerals.
options.label: ESA

options.text: The Dead Sea's shore is the lowest exposed land on Earth. You can stand more than 400 metres below ocean level with open sky above you.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Some Danube water reaches the North Sea. In southern Germany it sinks into limestone, resurfaces in a spring, and joins the Rhine. The main Danube continues east to the Black Sea.
options.label: Swabian Alb Geopark

options.text: Float downstream and the Danube takes you past four national capitals in order: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
options.label: International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River

options.text: Where the Danube meets the Black Sea, people have used the delta’s reeds to build their houses and fences.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Danube's drainage basin reaches into 19 countries, more than any other international river basin. A raindrop can start in a country the Danube never visits and still end up in the river.
options.label: icpdr.org

options.text: A magnitude-5.7 earthquake beneath Lake Taupō in 2022 sent two small tsunamis across this inland lake.
options.label: GNS Science

options.text: At Mine Bay, a 14-metre face looks out over the lake. Matahi Brightwell led the carving of his ancestor Ngātoroirangi into a cliff reached by water; the work took four years.
options.label: Destination Great Lake Taupō

options.text: Ngāti Tūwharetoa fishers lowered bundles of bracken fern to the lakebed. Freshwater crayfish sheltered among the fronds, and the fishers lifted the bundles into their canoes.
options.label: Earth Sciences New Zealand

options.text: New Zealand's largest lake fills the caldera of a volcano. The Waikato River, the country's longest, flows out of Lake Taupō on its way to the Tasman Sea.
options.label: doc.govt.nz

options.text: In one Māori account, the South Island is Māui’s canoe. The North Island is the fish he hauled up with a hook fashioned from his ancestor’s jawbone.
options.label: Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa

options.text: A male kākāpō digs a shallow bowl, settles into it at night, and booms for a mate. The hollow helps his calls resonate.
options.label: Department of Conservation

options.text: A newly hatched tuatara has a light-sensitive third eye on top of its head. Skin grows over it as the animal matures.
options.label: Department of Conservation

options.text: The plates beneath New Zealand swap roles. The Pacific Plate dives beneath the North Island, while near the south of the South Island the Australian Plate goes underneath the Pacific Plate.
options.label: gns.cri.nz

options.text: Baikal has its own landlocked seal. Some seals follow the Angara River out of the lake, but their home waters are deep inside Siberia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Baikal’s golomyanka gives birth to live young. The tail of the small species is so transparent that print can be read through it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Baikal holds roughly a fifth of the world’s unfrozen surface freshwater. Its basin has been collecting water for some 25 million years.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Baikal is the world's deepest lake. Its water surface is above sea level, but its deepest floor lies more than a kilometre below the level of the ocean.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The long ridges rising out of Lake Superior on Isle Royale began as lava flows over a billion years ago. Much later, an ice sheet scoured them into sharper relief.
options.label: NASA

options.text: From orbit, winter clouds over Lake Superior can look like streets. Cold air crossing the open water picks up moisture that falls as snow on the far shore.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Around 1900 there were no moose on Isle Royale. Biologists think the first arrivals swam across from the mainland.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Lake Superior alone holds more water than the other four Great Lakes combined. Its nearly 12,100 cubic kilometres slightly outweigh Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario put together.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Try to trace the Triangle on an official nautical chart and you hit a problem: there is no official boundary. Even the U.S. board that standardizes geographic names has no official entry for it.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The Gulf Stream runs through the Triangle. Along this swift current the weather can change violently, leaving a crew with very different conditions from the ones it set out in.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Navigators have reported odd compass readings in the Triangle. NOAA compared those reports with other regions and found that even the reported magnetic anomalies were unexceptional.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: One corner of the usual Miami–Bermuda–Puerto Rico triangle lies beside the deepest part of the Atlantic. The Puerto Rico Trench runs just north of the island.

options.text: Even the most inland parts of the UK are within about 125 km of tidal water. Look at how far the estuaries cut into the outline and the distance starts to make sense.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Medieval Europeans had two Britains to distinguish. Great Britain was the island across the Channel, and Little Britain was Brittany in what is now France.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: London still carries the name of the Roman settlement Londinium, founded on the site around AD 43. The meaning of that older name is uncertain.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The UK shares an island with another country. Its land border is on Ireland, across the sea from Great Britain, the island containing England, Scotland and Wales.
options.label: ordnancesurvey.co.uk

options.text: In the Chaîne des Puys, a line of volcanoes sits next to a great fault. Together they record an early stage of a continent pulling apart, right in the middle of France.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Burgundy a climat can be a particular plot of vines. Centuries of growers divided slopes by differences in soil, aspect and the wine each patch produced.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Roman aqueduct supplying Nîmes had to cross the Gardon valley. Its builders stacked three tiers of arches at the Pont du Gard to keep water high enough to flow onward by gravity.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: France's longest land border is with Brazil. It runs along the edge of French Guiana, an ocean away from Paris.
options.label: gov.br

options.text: In the western Caucasus, explorers descended more than two kilometres below the entrance of Krubera Cave. A second cave in the same region, Veryovkina, also passes the two-kilometre mark.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Tbilisi’s name points to something you can still feel there. The Georgian word for “warm” refers to the city’s sulfur springs.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The anthem adopted after Georgia’s Rose Revolution borrowed its music from two operas, Abesalom da Eteri and Daisi.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Georgia has rainforests on the Black Sea. In the Colchic lowlands, extraordinary rainfall sustains peat bogs in a warm temperate forest landscape.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Several of Germany’s great rivers carry water north. The exception begins in the Black Forest: the Danube sets off east across Europe.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: One possible origin for Berlin’s name is a Slavic word for swamp, a clue to the landscape along the Spree where the settlement grew.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The tune used for Germany’s national anthem began as an Austrian imperial anthem composed by Joseph Haydn.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The seabed off Germany's North Sea coast is part of the world's largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats. At low tide, the Wadden Sea turns into land you can walk on.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Greece sings only two stanzas of a much longer poem. The original Hymn to Liberty, inspired by the 1821 uprising, has 158.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The country’s Greek name, Elláda, and the English name Greece come by different routes. English inherited the Roman name Graecia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Trace Greece beyond its peninsulas and the outline breaks into an archipelago. The Factbook counts roughly 2,000 islands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Peloponnese is called a peninsula, but today you can sail all the way around it. The Corinth Canal cuts straight through its narrow land connection to the rest of Greece.
options.label: corinthcanal.com

options.text: Greenland’s ice sheet holds nearly seven percent of the world’s freshwater. Only Antarctica has a larger ice sheet.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Kalaallit Nunaat, the Greenlandic name for Greenland, means “land of the people.” The Norse name is traditionally credited to Erik the Red trying to attract settlers.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Greenland’s capital changed names in 1979. The Danish Godthåb meant “good hope,” while the Greenlandic Nuuk describes a cape.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: At Ilulissat, icebergs can run aground on a submerged sill at the mouth of the fjord. They may have to melt or break apart before they can reach the open sea.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The Danube once separated cities whose names you can still see on a map of Budapest. Buda stood on the west bank and Pest on the east before unification in 1873.

options.text: The Danube and Tisza divide Hungary into three broad stretches of country. One Hungarian name to look for on a river map is Duna, the Danube.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Hungarians call their country Magyarország, the country of the Magyars. The English name Hungary came through a different name used for peoples arriving on the eastern European steppes.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Central Europe's largest lake is shallow enough to average only about three metres deep. Hungary's Lake Balaton stretches almost 80 kilometres from end to end.

options.text: Listen to a Tosk choir in southern Albania and you can hear a single “e” held beneath two solo voices. The singers take turns breathing, so the note never breaks.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Outside Tirana, a bunker runs five storeys underground and contains 106 rooms. Visitors can now walk through it as a museum of Albania’s dictatorship.
options.label: Bunk’Art

options.text: In Albania’s northern highlands, a traditional garment called the xhubleta flares out in rippling folds like a bell. Its distinctive silhouette is built by hand from felt.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Vjosa crosses from Greece into Albania and runs freely to the Adriatic. In 2023 Albania made its stretch and several tributaries Europe's first wild river national park.
options.label: iucn.org

options.text: In Andorra’s national anthem the country itself speaks. Its history is sung in the first person.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The capital’s Catalan name, Andorra la Vella, means “Andorra the Old.”
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Andorra survives from a belt of frontier states that Charlemagne established in the Pyrenees. Its position between France and Spain goes back to that frontier.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: A single glacial valley system takes up almost a tenth of Andorra. The Madriu-Perafita-Claror landscape alone covers more than 4,000 hectares.

options.text: Near Baku, a line of flames burns along the foot of a hillside called Yanardag. The fuel seeps straight from the ground as natural gas.

options.text: On Gobustan’s dry hills, ancient artists carved boats and fish into the rock. One explanation is that the Caspian stood much higher then, almost turning the hills into islands.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Sheki and Basgal, makers of silk kelaghayi scarves print their designs with wooden stamps. A mixture containing resin and wax protects parts of the silk when the cloth is dyed.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Azerbaijan borders Turkey, but you cannot reach that border from Baku without leaving the country. The entire Turkish frontier belongs to the detached territory of Nakhchivan.

options.text: Belarus’s landscape bears the marks of moving ice. Glaciers scoured the terrain and helped leave it dotted with around 11,000 lakes.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: After the Soviet Union dissolved, Belarus kept the tune of its Soviet-era anthem. The replacement lyrics came in 2002.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The first part of Belarus comes from a Slavic word for white. The rest preserves the historical name Rus.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Białowieża Forest crosses from Belarus into Poland. It shelters Europe's largest free-roaming population of European bison in a fragment of the forest that once covered much of the continent.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: One tradition places the writing of Belgium’s anthem in a Brussels café during the 1830 revolution. Among the writers was an actor from the theatre associated with the uprising.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Belgium’s name recalls the Belgae, peoples whose territory stretched between the English Channel and the Rhine in antiquity.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The name Brussels preserves an older landscape: its Germanic roots refer to a dwelling and a marsh.

options.text: In Baarle, pockets of Belgium contain pockets of the Netherlands. The border winds through streets and even houses, where the front door can determine the address.

options.text: The song that became Bulgaria’s anthem was composed in 1885 by a student on his way to fight in the war with Serbia.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Bulgaria’s capital takes its name from a church. Parts of the Church of Saint Sofia may date as far back as the fourth century.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Bulgaria took its name from the Bulgars, a people of Central Asian origin who joined local Slavic inhabitants to form a state in the late seventh century.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The highest point anywhere on the Balkan Peninsula is in Bulgaria. Musala in the Rila Mountains rises to 2,925 metres, a little higher than Mount Olympus in Greece.

options.text: Off Croatia’s Adriatic coast, an atlas has to account for roughly 1,200 islands, islets, rocks and ridges. Most of the Adriatic’s islands lie on this side.

options.text: The words of Croatia’s anthem were written in 1835. The song was adopted officially in 1972, while Croatia was still part of Yugoslavia.

options.text: An old explanation of Zagreb’s name puts the settlement “beyond the ditch.” The two parts of the name describe where to find it.

options.text: You can now drive from the rest of Croatia to Dubrovnik without a border crossing. The Pelješac Bridge bypasses the strip of Bosnian coast that splits Croatia's mainland shoreline.

options.text: Around Žatec, the crop that shaped the landscape grows up wires. Fields, drying buildings and warehouses all belong to the long local history of growing hops for beer.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Kladruby nad Labem, people reshaped an Elbe floodplain to breed ceremonial carriage horses. Pastures, avenues and paddocks are part of the protected landscape.

options.text: Medieval Kutná Hora grew wealthy from what lay underneath it. Its silver mines helped turn an inland settlement into one of Bohemia's most important towns.

options.text: On the slopes of Králický Sněžník, water can set out for three different seas. The divides here separate the drainage basins of the Baltic, North and Black Seas.
options.label: visitczechia.com

options.text: The Danish mainland is only part of the country’s outline. More than 400 islands lie in the Danish archipelago.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Copenhagen’s name describes its old trade: its Danish roots mean a merchants’ harbour.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Denmark has two anthems of equal standing. A royal anthem dating to 1780 is used on occasions attended by royalty.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Kingdom of Denmark acquired a land border with Canada in 2022. It crosses a tiny Arctic island called Tartupaluk, or Hans Island, between Greenland and Ellesmere Island.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: Estonia and Finland sing different words to the same anthem melody. In Estonia the song was banned during Soviet rule.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Tallinn’s name has been traced to an Estonian expression for “Danish fort,” a reminder of the Danes who established a stronghold there in 1219.

options.text: Estonia’s low mainland gives way to an archipelago of more than 1,500 islands in the Baltic.

options.text: At Kaali on the island of Saaremaa, what looks like a little round woodland pond occupies the largest of a group of meteorite impact craters.

options.text: The Faroe Islands carry sheep in their name: the Old Norse words behind it mean “sheep islands.”
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Tórshavn, the Faroese capital, is named for Thor. Its name means “Thor’s harbour.”
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: People lived in the Faroes by about AD 500, centuries before the ninth-century Viking settlers arrived. The identity of those earlier islanders is uncertain.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Nowhere in the Faroe Islands is more than about five kilometres from the sea. Even the middle of the largest island is close to a fjord or an Atlantic shore.
options.label: visitfaroeislands.com

options.text: A desert lake can be a nursery. Nile crocodiles breed on Turkana’s islands, while submerged beds of pondweed shelter spawning fish in South Island’s muddy bays.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Koobi Fora, the ground beside the lake preserves early human relatives alongside molluscs and other animals. Researchers use the shells as well as the bones to reconstruct the landscape those humans inhabited.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On a map of bird migration, this arid part of Kenya is a water stop. Migrating waterbirds use the national parks around the world’s largest desert lake.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Turkana is the world's largest permanent desert lake. A great expanse of water survives in this arid basin because rivers bring in rain that fell elsewhere.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Researchers can date the rock paintings at Astuvansalmi using the lake itself. Changes in water level tell them when a painter could have reached a particular stretch of cliff.
options.label: saimaageopark.fi

options.text: A freshwater salmon lives in Saimaa. Its migrations take it between a lake and spawning rivers, so this population can complete its life without ever reaching salt water.

options.text: Some of the long, narrow ridges running through the lake are eskers. They mark places where streams deposited gravel in tunnels underneath an ice sheet.

options.text: Lake Saimaa looks like a cluster of lakes because its open basins are linked by narrow straits between thousands of islands. A continuous journey on water can weave through what looks like solid land on a small map.

options.text: A Lake Eyre dragon can make a living on the dry lakebed. This little lizard hunts ants and slips beneath the salt crust for shelter.

options.text: The flood that revives Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre can begin far outside South Australia. Monsoon rains in Queensland feed channels that carry the water across the arid interior.
options.label: National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia

options.text: As floodwater evaporates and turns to brine, most fish disappear. The Lake Eyre hardyhead can keep feeding and breeding in water saltier than the sea.
