options.text: Australia's lowest natural point is a lakebed you can often see. The floor of Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre lies roughly 15 metres below sea level and is usually exposed.
options.label: ga.gov.au

options.text: Deep Bay forms an almost circular hole in otherwise shallow Reindeer Lake. The water reaches about 220 metres down inside an ancient impact crater.
options.label: Lunar and Planetary Institute

options.text: Drillers investigating Reindeer Lake in the 1960s brought up shattered rock from beneath Deep Bay. The shock damage was evidence of an impact.
options.label: Lunar and Planetary Institute

options.text: The impact at Reindeer Lake forced rock back up at the centre of the crater. That central rise is still there, entirely hidden underwater.
options.label: Lunar and Planetary Institute

options.text: Reindeer Lake straddles Saskatchewan and Manitoba, but most of its water lies on the Saskatchewan side. Its outlet leads south to the Churchill River before the water turns towards Hudson Bay.
options.label: esask.uregina.ca

options.text: In winter the ice becomes a road between Yellowknife and Dettah. An early thaw in 2019 closed the crossing about a week ahead of its usual season.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Yellowknife builds a snow castle on Great Slave Lake. In 2019 warm weather forced its festival to close the castle for the first time in 24 years.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Water leaving the lake at its southwest end enters the Mackenzie River. The deepest lake in North America helps feed Canada’s longest river.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The East Arm of Great Slave Lake has cliffs with different faces. Tilted layers of bedrock slope down on one side and break off along steep fractures on the other.
options.label: gov.nt.ca

options.text: On the west shore of Lake Winnipegosis, seaside plantain grows far inland. Salty flats give plants usually found on northern coasts a foothold in the boreal forest.
options.label: Government of Manitoba

options.text: Springs beside this freshwater lake discharge brine. Its chemistry records groundwater dissolving rock salt and mixing with fresh water on the way up.
options.label: Government of Manitoba

options.text: You can walk from boreal vegetation into salt-tolerant meadow plants on the same lakeshore. As sheets of lakebed emerge, their poorly drained, salty soil sorts out what can grow there.
options.label: Government of Manitoba

options.text: Lake Winnipegosis is upstream of two much larger names on the map. Its water goes by the Waterhen River into Lake Manitoba, then onward into Lake Winnipeg.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: The Narrows separate a small, shallow southern basin from a much larger northern one. The southern basin averages only about nine metres deep.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: Winnipeg sits south of its namesake lake. The Red River carries water north from the city into the lake, away from the US border.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: The lake drains into Hudson Bay by the Nelson River. Water from the Canadian prairie thus rounds off its journey on the shore of a subarctic sea.
options.label: gov.mb.ca

options.text: Lake Winnipeg collects runoff from an area roughly forty times its own surface. A relatively shallow lake is the outlet for a basin reaching from the Rockies into the United States.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: On Onega's eastern shore, people pecked birds and other figures directly into the rock. The carvings form a World Heritage site with another group about 300 kilometres away on the White Sea.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Onega straddles a geological seam. Its basin sits partly on the ancient Baltic Shield and partly on the Russian Platform.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: The surface of this enormous inland lake sits only about 35 metres above the Baltic. Parts of its bed are well below sea level.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: Europe's second-largest lake drains straight towards its largest. Water leaving Lake Onega follows the Svir into Lake Ladoga before reaching the Baltic.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: Buller’s shearwaters reach the Gulf of Alaska from nesting grounds in New Zealand. A bird over these cold northern waters may have crossed most of the Pacific.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The gulf’s spring bloom is visible from space. In April 2017 two different satellite instruments recorded the growing phytoplankton bloom.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Black-footed albatrosses that breed in the western Hawaiian Islands forage here. Look for them around the edge of the gulf’s continental shelf.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Glaciers grind Alaska's rock into such fine powder that the Copper River carries it out to sea. From space its pale plume draws the Gulf of Alaska's coastal currents in colour.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: In June 1978 a wave driven by a disturbance in the atmosphere set Adriatic harbours surging on both the Croatian and Italian sides. The event is called a meteotsunami.
options.label: University of Split

options.text: A fisherman off Istria found the remains of a boat whose builders had sewn the hull together some 3,000 years ago. Part of the stitching survived on the Adriatic seabed.
options.label: French Ministry of Culture

options.text: The central Adriatic has a deep nursery called the Jabuka Pit. Young European hake gather there, and young Norway lobsters live more than 200 metres below the surface.
options.label: Convention on Biological Diversity

options.text: The Po River is slowly extending Italy into the Adriatic. Mud from its basin travels south along the Italian coast, leaving an underwater sediment belt on just one side of the sea.
options.label: iris.cnr.it

options.text: The seabed between Africa and Arabia has been pulling apart for roughly 30 million years. Today the Red Sea fills that growing rift.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Even in the Red Sea’s unusually salty water, researchers have counted around 260 species of coral.
options.label: NASA

options.text: A photograph taken above the Sudanese coast in 1993 caught a satellite flying free over the Red Sea. The crew of Discovery had released it by robot arm and later picked it up again.
options.label: NASA

options.text: No permanently flowing river replenishes the Red Sea. Water lost to evaporation has to be replaced through a narrow southern gateway, the Bab el-Mandeb.
options.label: repository.kaust.edu.sa

options.text: The narrow finger of Afghanistan that reaches toward China is the Wakhan Corridor. It holds the country’s highest peaks.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Hindu Kush cuts diagonally across the country, separating the northern provinces from much of the rest of Afghanistan.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Between the Russian and British empires, the territory of Afghanistan served as a buffer. Afghanistan secured control of its own foreign affairs in 1919.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Afghanistan's longest river never finds the ocean. The Helmand flows southwest from the Hindu Kush into a chain of desert wetlands on the Iranian frontier.
options.label: unomaha.edu

options.text: In the Saharan oases of Touat and Tidikelt, dividing water is a specialist trade. Water measurers calculate each grower’s share of the flow from underground channels called foggaras.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tin Bider looks like a dent in satellite images of the Algerian Sahara. Part of the illusion is the angle of the light. The six-kilometre crater actually stands above the land to its south.
options.label: NASA

options.text: In the M’Zab Valley, five fortified towns each have a summer counterpart in a palm grove. Moving to the shade for the hottest months is built into the layout of the settlements.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Algeria is Africa's largest country by area. Roughly four-fifths of it is desert, so a map of where people live looks much smaller than the political map.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Off Taʻū, divers call one patch of reef the Valley of Giants. Its largest coral colony, nicknamed Big Momma, measures about 41 metres around. Sanctuary scientists estimate it is over 500 years old.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Look up in daylight and you may see a peʻa vao soaring on warm air. This Samoan fruit bat can even carry its young in flight.
options.label: National Park Service

options.text: The villages own the land in the National Park of American Samoa. They granted the park service a 50-year lease, keeping the land in Samoan hands.
options.label: National Park Service

options.text: Ships entering Pago Pago sail into the remains of a volcano. Part of its rim collapsed and the sea flooded the opening, leaving Tutuila with a deep harbour ringed by steep slopes.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Angola takes its name from a royal title. Portuguese visitors heard the rulers of Ndongo called ngola and applied the word to the land.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Follow Angola’s coast north and you leave the country before re-entering it. A strip of the Democratic Republic of the Congo separates Cabinda from the rest of Angola.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Luanda once had a much longer Portuguese name, São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda. The last part survived as the name of Angola’s capital.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Some rain falling in Angola never makes it to the sea. The highlands supply the Okavango, which spreads into a great inland delta in Botswana's Kalahari.
options.label: nationalgeographic.org

options.text: Antarctica is the highest continent on average. It is also the driest, despite having a surface largely made of frozen water.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The South Pole gets sunlight around the clock in summer. Over the same stretch of summer time it can receive more solar energy at the surface than the equator.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The name Antarctica gives a direction in Greek. It means the place opposite the Arctic.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Earth's driest continent holds most of its fresh water. Antarctica receives very little precipitation, yet enough snow has accumulated over time to build its enormous ice sheet.
options.label: bas.ac.uk

options.text: Antigua was named for a church in Seville. Columbus borrowed the name Santa María la Antigua on his second Atlantic voyage in 1493.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Antigua’s shoreline folds into numerous natural harbours. On Barbuda, the large harbour is on the western side.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Archaeological settlement on these islands goes back to about 2400 BC, thousands of years before European sailing charts showed them.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Barbuda's Codrington Lagoon is sheltered by a narrow sand barrier. Its mangroves hold one of the Caribbean's great breeding colonies of magnificent frigatebirds.
options.label: internationalconservation.org

options.text: An Armenian khachkar begins as local stone. The maker uses hammers, chisels and fine-pointed tools to cut a cross and its surrounding ornament into the surface.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Traditional Armenian lavash can be stored for up to six months. The same thin bread that keeps so long can be wrapped around fresh greens or cheese.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The fortress of Erebuni stood on the site of present-day Yerevan in 782 BC. One explanation traces the modern city’s name to that fortress.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Armenia is landlocked yet has a vast high-altitude shore. Lake Sevan, nearly two kilometres above the sea, is the largest lake in the Lesser Caucasus.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: There was a gold rush in Aruba in the nineteenth century. Gold mining, oil refining and tourism each had a turn shaping the island’s economy.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Aruba’s capital translates as “Orange City.” In 1824 Oranjestad was named for the Dutch royal House of Orange-Nassau.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Aruba is a riverless Caribbean island. Atlantic trade winds blow across the low terrain and temper its tropical heat.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: At Dos Playa, rocks on dry land preserve round pillows of lava. They formed when molten rock cooled underwater, long before this part of Aruba was a shore.
options.label: coleccion.aw

options.text: Barbados’s name means “the bearded ones.” One explanation points to the island’s fig trees, whose hanging growth resembles beards.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Before it was Bridgetown, the settlement beside Carlisle Bay was called Indian Bridge. A bridge gave the capital a landmark early enough to appear in its 1628 name.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Enslaved Africans worked the sugar plantations that made this small eastern island a leading early producer in the Caribbean sugar trade.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Barbados sits east of the main arc of the Lesser Antilles, out towards the open Atlantic. It is the easternmost island country in the Caribbean.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Benin’s capital has a Portuguese name on the coast of West Africa. Porto-Novo simply means “new port.”
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The old national name Dahomey preserved the name of an earlier kingdom, Dan Homé, in what is now southern Benin.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Sandbanks line Benin’s shore. A coastline open to the Gulf of Guinea offered ships little in the way of natural harbour shelter.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: At Ganvié on Lake Nokoué, the streets are waterways and houses stand on stilts. Building a settlement out on the lake offered refuge during the slave trade.
options.label: benintourisme.bj

options.text: English colonists bound for Virginia in 1609 were shipwrecked on Bermuda. A failed Atlantic crossing helped establish the island’s first settlement.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Bermuda gets ample rain, yet its archipelago has neither rivers nor freshwater lakes.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The islands took their name from Juan de Bermúdez, a Spanish captain who explored them in the early 1500s, about a century before the English settlement.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Stalactites hang underwater in Bermuda's caves. They could only have grown in air, so their present depth records a time when the sea stood lower.
options.label: environment.bm

options.text: In Dzongkha, Bhutan is Druk Yul, the Land of the Dragon. The English name may instead preserve a Sanskrit reference to the edge of Tibet.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: At Drametse in Bhutan, a drum dance brings together sixteen masked dancers and a ten-member ensemble. The masks are part of the dance itself.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bhutan’s position on the map is also a position on a route. Several passes through the Himalayas link the approaches from India and Tibet.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: Bhutan has put a floor under the amount of green on its map. Its constitution requires at least 60 per cent of the country to remain under forest cover for all time.
options.label: redd.dofps.gov.bt

options.text: Brazil was named for a tree. Brazilwood grew along the coast and yielded a deep red dye.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: In a capoeira circle, the master sets the rhythm of the game with chants and a single-string percussion instrument.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Brazil touches every South American country except two. Neither Ecuador nor Chile shares a border with it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived country profile)

options.text: The Atlantic can send a breaking wave upstream into Brazilian rivers. On the Amazon estuary this tidal bore is known as the pororoca.
options.label: en.aguasamazonicas.org

options.text: Sail into the bay at Santorini and you are inside a volcano. The cliffs holding up the white-roofed towns are the rim of a flooded caldera.
options.label: NASA

options.text: At Akrotiri, volcanic ash buried a Bronze Age town on the Aegean. The same eruption that transformed the island also preserved the settlement.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The dark islands in the middle of Santorini’s bay are much younger than the pale cliffs around them. Lava began building them roughly fourteen centuries after the great eruption.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Water from the Black Sea reaches the Aegean through two straits and a sea in between. It passes through the Bosporus, crosses the Sea of Marmara and emerges from the Dardanelles.
options.label: seapower.navy.gov.au

options.text: Trade routes here had a built-in return season. The monsoon reverses its winds over the Arabian Sea, and the direction of surface currents changes with them.
options.label: NASA

options.text: A bloom caught by satellite in 2019 was made by Noctiluca, a single-celled organism that can thrive in oxygen-poor water. From space, the bloom coloured a swath of sea.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Winter on the Tibetan Plateau helps set the table for microscopic life offshore. Cold, dry air blowing out from Asia cools the sea surface and changes how nutrients reach sunlit water.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Below the sunlit Arabian Sea lies one of the ocean's great oxygen-poor zones. The surface is productive enough that sinking organic material consumes much of the oxygen below as it decays.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Wreckage from a ship crushed off Siberia washed up in Greenland. Fridtjof Nansen took that as a clue to a current and deliberately froze his own ship, Fram, into the ice to ride the drift.
options.label: National Snow and Ice Data Center

options.text: A narwhal’s spiral tusk starts as a tooth. In young males, the left upper tooth usually grows straight through the front of the jaw.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: To find out how long a Greenland shark could live, researchers dated the centres of the animals’ eye lenses. The results put their lifespan at a minimum of 272 years.
options.label: Science

options.text: The Arctic is the smallest ocean. Unlike the ocean around Antarctica, it has continents nearly encircling a sea, with the North Pole itself afloat over deep water.
options.label: oceanservice.noaa.gov

options.text: The Swedish warship Vasa survived for centuries partly because of where it sank. The brackish water around the wreck kept wood-eating shipworms from destroying its hull.
options.label: Vasa Museum

options.text: Along Finland’s Baltic shore, islands still rise out of the sea. The crust is rebounding from an ice sheet that once pressed down on it with kilometres of ice.
options.label: NASA

options.text: A summer map of the Baltic can show swirls that look painted onto the water. They are blooms of microscopic organisms, large enough in aggregate for satellites to follow.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Follow Baltic water from the Danish straits to the head of the Gulf of Bothnia and it gets progressively fresher. A narrow connection to the ocean struggles to replace the salt diluted by hundreds of rivers.
options.label: stateofthebalticsea.helcom.fi

options.text: Banda Api is an island inside a much larger volcano. Its cone rises within a roughly seven-kilometre-wide caldera, most of which lies underwater.
options.label: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

options.text: In May 1988, two eruption columns rose from Banda Api at the same time. Lava reached the sea while people on nearby islands watched and evacuated.
options.label: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

options.text: The spice trade left volcanologists an unusual gift. Portuguese and Dutch traffic through the Banda Islands helped produce a long written record of the island volcano’s activity.
options.label: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program

options.text: The Banda Sea holds the deepest known patch of ocean floor outside an ocean trench. The Weber Deep drops roughly 7.2 kilometres into a basin inside Indonesia's curved island arc.
options.label: researchportalplus.anu.edu.au

options.text: Tiny organisms can turn the Barents Sea a milky turquoise. Each coccolithophore carries reflective plates made of calcite, the same mineral found in chalk.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Some Arctic ports on the Barents Sea stay free of ice year-round. Water carried north from the Atlantic supplies the heat.
options.label: NASA

options.text: A front runs through the sea itself. Relatively warm, salty Atlantic water meets colder, fresher Arctic water inside the shallow Barents basin.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Much of the Barents Sea is continental shelf. Atlantic warmth keeps the southwest largely ice-free even as the northern part of the same shallow sea freezes.
options.label: npolar.no

options.text: From Little Diomede in Alaska you can look across the water into tomorrow. The International Date Line passes between it and Russia’s Big Diomede.
options.label: NASA

options.text: When glaciers locked up enough seawater, today’s strait became a land connection roughly 1,000 miles wide. The ice-age “bridge” was a landscape in its own right.
options.label: US National Park Service

options.text: The Pacific’s only direct seawater passage into the Arctic is remarkably shallow. Water from a deep ocean must cross a sill only about 50 metres deep.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: North America and Asia were connected here because a surprisingly shallow shelf lies beneath the strait. A sea-level fall of roughly 50 metres can expose the land now hidden under its waters.
options.label: npgallery.nps.gov

options.text: A volcano north of Grenada has a name fit for a sea shanty: Kick-’em-Jenny. Its summit is underwater, and instruments across the Caribbean have recorded acoustic signals from its vicinity.
options.label: US Geological Survey

options.text: The Caribbean shore of Belize shelters a barrier reef, offshore atolls and hundreds of sand cays. Its mangroves and lagoons are part of the same protected reef system.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Nearly five kilometres down in the Cayman Trough, researchers found a plume rising more than a kilometre above the Beebe vents. It carried copper-rich fluid up from a spreading crack in the Caribbean seafloor.
options.label: Nature Communications

options.text: Between Jamaica and the Cayman Islands, the Caribbean floor drops more than seven kilometres into the Cayman Trough. Tropical shallows sit next to the deepest part of the whole sea.
options.label: cigarchives.gov.ky

options.text: At a depth of 2,800 metres, researchers found a swimming worm with so many squid-like appendages that they nicknamed it the squidworm.
options.label: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

options.text: A robot near the bottom of the Celebes Sea filmed an almost black comb jelly. Many of its relatives in brighter surface waters are nearly transparent.
options.label: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

options.text: A diver collecting in the top 30 metres of the sea photographed a juvenile boxfish just a centimetre long. Its portrait came from the sunlit layer above a basin more than five kilometres deep.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The Celebes Sea is part of a sea route that water itself takes between oceans. Pacific water enters from the north and turns south through the Makassar Strait on its way to the Indian Ocean.
options.label: whoi.edu

options.text: Ships in the western Coral Sea reported floating mats of microscopic organisms up to two metres thick. A shuttle crew later photographed the sheen at the edge of a bloom.
options.label: NASA

options.text: In surveys of Coral Sea reefs, olive sea snakes accounted for roughly nine out of ten sea snakes observed. Survey teams repeatedly found them on southern reefs while finding none at several northern sites.
options.label: Parks Australia

options.text: Some Coral Sea islands barely rise above the water, yet their sand is important nesting ground. Green turtles and breeding seabirds share these remote cays.
options.label: Parks Australia

options.text: Along one edge of the Coral Sea is the world's largest coral reef ecosystem. The Great Barrier Reef stretches more than 2,000 kilometres along northeastern Australia.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Northern Australia's coastline makes a deep U between Arnhem Land and Cape York. The water enclosed by those two great projections is the Gulf of Carpentaria.
options.label: marinemammalhabitat.org

options.text: Dugongs graze the gulf's underwater seagrass meadows. A cyclone can strip a feeding ground and send the animals along the coast in search of another one.
options.label: marinemammalhabitat.org

options.text: The gulf has island groups on opposite flanks of its southern arc. The Sir Edward Pellew Islands lie off the Northern Territory and the Wellesley Islands off Queensland.
options.label: marinemammalhabitat.org

options.text: There are reefs and rocky pinnacles hidden under the muddy waters of the Gulf of Carpentaria. In the marine park north of Mornington Island, even the deepest water is only about 70 metres deep.
options.label: australianmarineparks.gov.au

options.text: Zero latitude and zero longitude meet in open water here. NOAA’s tropical Atlantic archive even has a buoy station indexed at the coordinate pair 0°, 0°.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Four species of sea turtle come ashore on São Tomé, a volcanic island rising out of the gulf. On the same island’s forest floor lives a dwarf ibis found nowhere else.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The research buoy once stationed where the equator crosses the prime meridian was moved west in 2021. Piracy in the gulf had made servicing the mooring harder.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The volcanic line running through Cameroon continues offshore into the Gulf of Guinea. Bioko, Príncipe, São Tomé and Annobón mark its course across the sea.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In a cold winter, seawater at the surface of the western Labrador Sea can mix to more than two kilometres deep. Few stretches of ocean have such direct contact between the surface and the depths.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Icebergs from the north pass through the Labrador Sea on their way to the Grand Banks. The currents along Baffin Island and Labrador form successive legs of the journey.
options.label: Government of Canada

options.text: Part of the Labrador Sea can freeze in spring after staying open through winter. A fresh surface layer and a subsequent cold snap can make ice possible where winter mixing had kept it away.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Labrador Sea is a stranded ocean-opening project. Its floor preserves a spreading ridge where Greenland and North America once pulled apart before spreading stopped here.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: For centuries, pearls lifted from oyster beds in the gulf financed houses on Bahrain. The World Heritage site preserves both the underwater beds and buildings on shore.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: An invention in Japan helped transform life on the Persian Gulf. Cultured pearls undermined Bahrain’s natural-pearl trade in the twentieth century.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In July 2008 a storm carried dust from Iraq out over the gulf. From space, pale arcs in the air appeared alongside patterns in the water northeast of Qatar.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Persian Gulf averages only about 35 metres deep. Intense evaporation turns some of that shallow water into dense brine that flows out beneath incoming water at Hormuz.
options.label: www2.whoi.edu

options.text: Even eels that grow up in Japanese freshwater travel far out to sea to reproduce. Researchers collected their eggs beside the West Mariana Ridge around the new moon.
options.label: Nature Communications

options.text: At a submarine volcano in the Mariana arc, cold drops of liquid carbon dioxide escape from a vent field alongside hot fluid. Researchers named the site Champagne.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Two eel species share a spawning area here. Their larvae ride away from the same region, yet eventually reach habitats spread from Japan to Indonesia.
options.label: Nature Communications

options.text: At the eastern edge of the Philippine Sea Plate, the Pacific Plate bends down beneath it. That contact traces the Mariana Trench, home to the deepest known point in the ocean.
options.label: usgs.gov

options.text: Some waves crossing the northern South China Sea travel inside the water column. Their surface signatures are clear enough for researchers to trace them in satellite imagery.
options.label: NASA

options.text: A reef in the South China Sea contains a deep vertical cavity called Yongle Blue Hole. Researchers sampling the water found that oxygen disappears below about 100 metres.
options.label: Frontiers in Marine Science

options.text: At Dongsha Atoll, even waves travelling below the sea surface can bounce back. Researchers documented internal waves reflecting from the atoll using satellite observations.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The southern South China Sea spreads over a drowned continental shelf. At ice-age low stands enough of the Sunda Shelf emerged to connect Borneo to mainland Southeast Asia.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: For generations, Indonesian fishers used freshwater wells on the islands of Ashmore Reef. The islands also preserve graves and traces of cooking sites from those voyages.
options.label: Australian environment department

options.text: At Ashmore Reef, tiny patches of land in the Timor Sea support nesting seabirds and turtles. On land, invasive tropical fire ants threaten chicks and turtle hatchlings.
options.label: Parks Australia

options.text: Ashmore Reef was known for its many sea snakes. When scientists carried out an extensive reef health survey, they searched the shallows and failed to find one.
options.label: Parks Australia

options.text: Australia's broad continental shelf ends abruptly in the Timor Trough. Deep water lies close to Timor even though much of the sea on the Australian side is shallow.
options.label: aph.gov.au

options.text: A current can circle Antarctica without meeting land. The Antarctic Circumpolar Current threads the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans into a single loop.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: A blue whale can grow to be the largest animal on Earth on a diet made up almost entirely of krill. The little crustaceans graze on microscopic algae in these waters.
options.label: Source

options.text: Pack ice crushed Shackleton’s Endurance in 1915. When a search team found it on the Weddell Sea floor in 2022, the ship’s name and the star on its stern were still visible.
options.label: Source

options.text: A latitude serves as the northern edge of the Southern Ocean in a widely used definition. Crossing 60° south can put a ship in a new ocean without passing a cape or a strait.
options.label: oceanservice.noaa.gov

options.text: Bryde’s whales here have been filmed standing almost upright with their mouths open at the surface. Fish tumble across the lower jaw while the whale holds still.
options.label: Source

options.text: Archaeologists excavated a seagoing ship eight kilometres inland from today’s gulf. Its builders had stitched the hull planks together with rope.
options.label: Source

options.text: At Ban Khun Samut Chin the shoreline retreated through a village. Families moved inland, leaving the Buddhist temple standing out at the water’s edge.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Gulf of Thailand is a flooded hollow on the Sunda Shelf. It averages about 45 metres deep, and even its deepest water is less than 100 metres deep.
options.label: sciencedirect.com

options.text: In 1977 researchers diving near the Galápagos found a thriving community around hot vents on the dark seabed. Microbes using chemicals from the vents fed the other animals.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: A boat can sail through the Great Pacific Garbage Patch without seeing an island of rubbish. Much of the plastic is in small fragments spread through the water.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: At Point Nemo, the three nearest pieces of land are each about 2,688 kilometres away. The spot takes its name from Jules Verne’s submarine captain.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Gather every continent and island into one patch and the Pacific would still cover more area. This single ocean basin is larger than all Earth's dry land combined.
options.label: origin.oceanexplorer.noaa.gov

options.text: Most of the mountain range dividing the Atlantic lies underwater. In Iceland it rises through the surface, where you can walk across the rift between the plates.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In 1866 a lasting telegraph cable connected Valentia Island in Ireland to a Newfoundland village called Heart’s Content. Messages that once crossed by ship could travel through a wire on the ocean floor.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Atlantic contains a sea whose boundaries move. Four currents enclose the floating seaweed of the Sargasso Sea, giving it a perimeter without a coastline.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The North Atlantic is saltier at the surface than the North Pacific. Oceans that share a continuous body of water can still have measurably different salt concentrations.
options.label: mynasadata.larc.nasa.gov

options.text: At the Kairei deep-sea vents, a snail grows iron sulphide minerals on the scales covering its foot. Its armour incorporates minerals from the vent environment.
options.label: Source

options.text: South of Sri Lanka, Earth’s uneven gravity makes the ocean surface sit lower than it would on a uniform planet. Satellites can measure this broad hollow in the sea.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The tsunami that began off Sumatra in 2004 left a trace far outside the Indian Ocean. Tide gauges around the world recorded its passage.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The Indian Ocean runs into Asia before it can reach the Arctic. Across its northern end, monsoon winds reverse with the seasons and major surface currents reverse with them.
options.label: pmel.noaa.gov

options.text: For polar bears on the western shore, summer takes away the hunting ground itself. When the sea ice melts, the bears come ashore and live largely on stored fat until freeze-up.
options.label: Government of Canada

options.text: From orbit the Belcher Islands look like loops drawn in ink across the bay. The long, thin islands trace the folds of ancient layers of rock.
options.label: NASA

options.text: You can find old Hudson Bay beaches inland and uphill. The crust is still rising after the great ice sheets melted and lifted their weight from it.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Gravity is unusually weak around Hudson Bay. Part of the anomaly records ice that vanished thousands of years ago, because Earth's interior is still responding to losing its weight.
options.label: nature.com

options.text: Near the White Sea, prehistoric artists carved boats and sea hunts into bare rock. The hunters and their prey are still visible thousands of years later.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some White Sea belugas return to the same summer gathering grounds so predictably that researchers on the Solovetsky Islands have watched them from shore over successive years.
options.label: Source

options.text: On the Solovetsky Islands, monks linked lakes with canals. A monastery in the White Sea built itself a freshwater transport and supply network.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The White Sea has a literal throat. Its narrow Gorlo funnels the tidal exchange between the inner sea and the Barents Sea beyond it.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Off the Lofoten Islands lies the Røst Reef, an immense coral reef growing in deep, cold water beyond the reach of sunlight.
options.label: Source

options.text: About 8,000 years ago part of the seabed off Norway slid downhill. The tsunami it sent across the sea left layers of sand on the Scottish coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: Herring spend the feeding season where Arctic and Atlantic waters meet. When the shoals head for their Norwegian wintering grounds, killer whales follow them.
options.label: Source

options.text: Water heading into the Arctic from the Atlantic crosses the Norwegian Sea. Its warm northward route carries ocean heat past the Arctic Circle along Norway.
options.label: awi.de

options.text: Even in summer the Celtic Sea can hold a pool of cold water near its bed. A lid of warmer water keeps it apart from the surface.
options.label: Source

options.text: Near the edge of the continental shelf, long ridges of sand rise as much as 60 metres from the seabed. Some run for up to 200 kilometres.
options.label: Source

options.text: Satellite tags revealed journeys through the Celtic Sea by basking sharks seen off western Scotland. The same animal can use waters off Scotland and southwest England.
options.label: Source

options.text: Sail southwest from Ireland and the Celtic Sea stretches out as a shallow shelf. At its outer edge the seabed falls away into deep Atlantic water at the Porcupine Seabight and Goban Spur.
options.label: nwwac.org

options.text: Sonar revealed enormous hollows beneath the Strait of Dover. Researchers traced them to waterfalls spilling from an ice-dammed lake when a land bridge still joined Britain and France.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Channel Tunnel is actually three tunnels. A service tunnel runs between the two railway tunnels, with cross-passages every 375 metres.
options.label: Source

options.text: The first recorded unaided swim across the Channel took 21 hours and 45 minutes. Matthew Webb made it from England to France in 1875.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel, the English Channel has tides large enough to redraw the coastline in hours. Water sweeps across sandbanks around an abbey perched above them on a rock.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Capbreton Canyon carries sediment downhill beneath the waves. Repeated surveys caught changes on its floor after sediment moved through the canyon.
options.label: Source

options.text: Deep canyons off the French coast shelter cold-water coral communities. Their branching colonies grow far below the sunlit surface of the bay.
options.label: Source

options.text: Where rivers pour into the Bay of Biscay, their plumes help shape the spawning grounds of anchovies. The fish gather in particular patches of water on the shelf.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Bay of Biscay opened as Iberia rotated away from what is now France. The bend in Europe's Atlantic coast records a vanished spreading centre.
options.label: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: A submerged ridge between Sicily and Tunisia divides the Mediterranean into two main basins. The eastern basin covers almost twice the area of the western one.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: The opening of the Suez Canal gave Red Sea animals a route into the Mediterranean. Some have spread far beyond the canal along its eastern shores.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: The Black Sea has a winding route to the Mediterranean. Water passes the Bosporus, the Sea of Marmara and the Dardanelles before it reaches the Aegean.
options.label: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov

options.text: The Mediterranean loses more water to evaporation than it gains from rain and rivers. Atlantic water streams in at the surface at Gibraltar while denser, saltier Mediterranean water escapes underneath.
options.label: doi.org

options.text: Woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island for thousands of years after they disappeared from most of the mainland. Some were still alive around 4,000 years ago.
options.label: Source

options.text: Open water can persist beside Wrangel Island even when ice covers the sea around it. These recurring openings are called polynyas.
options.label: Source

options.text: Pacific eiders nest on tundra around this sea, including Wrangel Island. After breeding, they travel through the Chukchi Sea to spend winter in the Bering Sea.
options.label: Source

options.text: Between the New Siberian Islands and Wrangel Island, the Arctic Ocean spreads across a broad, shallow shelf. The East Siberian Sea covers land that was exposed during lower ice-age seas.
options.label: pame.is

options.text: Rock worn off the Himalayas ends up far out beneath the bay. Rivers deliver it to the Bengal Fan, a submarine pile of sediment stretching about 3,000 kilometres.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the northern bay, rain and river water can leave a layer of fresher water only about 15 metres deep floating on the saltier sea.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the Sundarbans at the head of the bay, tigers swim long distances between mangrove islands. Fish and crabs are among the prey they take in this tidal forest.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A layer of relatively fresh water floats on the Bay of Bengal. Monsoon rain and river discharge make its surface markedly fresher than that of the Arabian Sea on the other side of India.
options.label: drs.nio.res.in

options.text: In Toyama Bay, firefly squid rise from deep water and flash blue in the dark. Fishing boats go out before dawn during the spring season.
options.label: Source

options.text: Cold air leaving Siberia picks up moisture as it crosses this sea. By the time it hits Japan’s mountains, it can unload extraordinary amounts of snow.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Bluefin tuna, yellowtail and flying squid travel north on the warm Tsushima Current. In autumn the migration reverses toward the spawning grounds.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Sea of Japan is kilometres deep, but its doorways are shallow. Water moving between this basin and the surrounding seas has to cross much shallower straits.
options.label: journals.ametsoc.org

options.text: On their migration along the Asian coast, spoon-billed sandpipers stop to feed on the Yellow Sea mudflats. Look closely at one and even the tip of its tiny bill flares out like a spoon.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In satellite pictures, turquoise and tan swirls can run across this shallow sea. Tides and waves stir fine sediment off the seabed and suspend it in the water.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Korean tidal flats, or getbol, are home to mud octopuses, fiddler crabs and ghost crabs. At low tide a whole stretch of their seafloor becomes dry enough to walk across.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Yellow Sea takes its colour and its name from sediment. Rivers carry such fine mineral grains into this shallow sea that tides can keep them suspended long after they reach salt water.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: The Lord Howe Island stick insect was feared extinct. In 2001 a team found survivors on Ball’s Pyramid, a steep rock spire 16 kilometres out to sea.
options.label: Source

options.text: A chain of 16 extinct volcanoes runs roughly 2,000 kilometres through the Tasman and Coral seas. Some peaks rise more than four kilometres above the surrounding seabed.
options.label: Source

options.text: In 2002 astronauts photographed a storm over the Tasman Sea with features of both a tropical cyclone and a higher-latitude storm. The shuttle crew could see the curve of its cloud bands from orbit.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Part of the Tasman Sea covers a continent. The Lord Howe Rise is a broad, submerged piece of Zealandia extending northwest from New Zealand towards Australia.
options.label: rsnz.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: In 2019 a crew paddled a dugout canoe from Taiwan to Yonaguni to test how early voyagers might have crossed. It took just over 45 hours, with the island below the horizon for most of the trip.
options.label: National Museum of Nature and Science, Japan

options.text: Off Jeju, haenyeo divers gather abalone and sea urchins on a single breath. When they surface, you can hear the distinctive sound they make as they take in air for the next dive.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Where the Yangtze empties into the East China Sea, divers found a wooden Qing-era merchant vessel. In the murky estuary, one of the few photographs they could take showed porcelain still sitting in rows.
options.label: Shanghai Municipal Government

options.text: In summer, freshwater from China's Yangtze can travel across the East China Sea towards Korea's Jeju Island. Its low-salinity surface plume crosses national waters.
options.label: frontiersin.org

options.text: In 1931 a fishing trawler hauled up a barbed antler point from the North Sea. Someone had fashioned it when dry land still stretched between Britain and the continent.
options.label: Source

options.text: Beneath the Ekofisk oil field, the reservoir rock compacted as oil was extracted. In the middle of the field the seabed itself has sunk about ten metres.
options.label: Source

options.text: Twice a day the North Sea uncovers the Wadden Sea mudflats. Migrating birds stop there in their millions to feed on the animals in the exposed sediment.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: An arm of the North Sea became a freshwater lake in the twentieth century. The Dutch closed the Afsluitdijk across the Zuiderzee, creating the IJsselmeer behind it.
options.label: rijkswaterstaat.nl

options.text: Sea ice forms as far south as Japan here. Fresh water from the Amur makes a surface layer that can freeze before the saltier water underneath.
options.label: Source

options.text: The drift ice off Shiretoko helps feed bears on land. Winter mixing supplies nutrients for spring plankton, which feed a food web that sends salmon up forest streams.
options.label: Source

options.text: Off Sakhalin Island, western gray whales return in summer and autumn to feed on animals living on the seabed. This stretch of the Sea of Okhotsk is a vital feeding ground for them.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The curved chain of the Kuril Islands forms a gate between the Sea of Okhotsk and the open Pacific. Ocean water passes through the gaps between the volcanoes.
options.label: meetings.pices.int

options.text: A mud volcano off Azerbaijan built an island in early 2023. Satellites watched the Caspian reclaim it almost entirely by the end of 2024.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The Caspian has its own species of seal. In winter the seals gather on ice in the shallow north of this landlocked lake to give birth and nurse their pups.
options.label: Source

options.text: On the eastern shore, a narrow channel feeds a salty lagoon called Garabogazköl. A dam closed the channel in 1980 and the lagoon nearly dried up. In 1992 the dam came down.
options.label: NASA

options.text: The world's largest lake ends below the level of the world ocean. Rivers pour into the Caspian, but there is no natural river carrying its water out to sea.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: On Taquile Island, you can wear the farming calendar. Weavers make a wide belt whose designs record the year’s agricultural work and rituals.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some of the islands on Titicaca are built from plants. Uros communities make floating islands out of totora reeds, high in the Andes between Peru and Bolivia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: More than 25 rivers feed Titicaca, but just one, the Desaguadero, drains it. Most of the water that leaves this cold mountain lake goes straight into the air.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A narrow waist almost divides Titicaca in two. Boats cross the Tiquina Strait between its large, deep northwestern basin and its much smaller southeastern basin.
options.label: esa.int

options.text: Tanganyika has a fish that plays the cuckoo’s trick underwater. A cichlid gathering her eggs into her mouth can scoop up catfish eggs too. The catfish hatch first.
options.label: Source

options.text: A passenger ship reached this landlocked lake in crates. A German shipyard built the Graf Goetzen, took it apart for transport, and sent the pieces to be reassembled on Tanganyika.
options.label: Source

options.text: Some freshwater snails here grow such ornate shells that biologists call them “sea-like.” Tanganyika has dozens of snail species found nowhere else.
options.label: Source

options.text: Lake Tanganyika stretches for more than 650 kilometres along an African rift. It is the world's longest freshwater lake, yet you are seldom far from one of its two long shores.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: You can cross from nearly fresh water to salty water without leaving the lake. The Ili River freshens the western basin, and a narrow strait limits how much mixes into the east.
options.label: NASA

options.text: At the lake’s southern edge, the Ili River fans into a wetland in the desert. The same protected area shelters goitered gazelles, marbled polecats and white-headed ducks.
options.label: Source

options.text: Balkhash spends winter under ice. A satellite passing over in March 2026 caught strips of turquoise water opening through the white ice cover.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Water from mountains in China arrives in Kazakhstan and ends its journey at Balkhash. The lake has no outlet to the sea, so water that enters it leaves mainly by evaporation.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: The Arctic Circle cuts through Great Bear Lake. Its northern and southern shores lie on opposite sides of the latitude used to define the Arctic.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Five long arms meet in a central basin. Water leaving by the Great Bear River starts its outward journey from the southwest arm, called Keith Arm.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: In summer, warmer water can build up in the arms while the middle stays cold. A temperature reading from the shore can give a very misleading picture of the lake.
options.label: agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com

options.text: Great Bear Lake is the largest lake entirely within Canada. The Canadian Great Lakes with larger surface areas all have a US shore as well.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: When wind piles water up toward Buffalo, the level can fall at Toledo, at the other end of the lake. The water then sloshes back, a motion called a seiche.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: On Kelleys Island, you can see deep grooves in the bedrock where a glacier once scraped across what is now Lake Erie.
options.label: Source

options.text: Lake Erie helped snow fall on Buffalo while the trees were still in leaf during the “October Surprise.” Cold air crossing the warmer lake picked up the water that fell as heavy snow downwind.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: Erie is the shallowest of the five Great Lakes and the quickest to flush. Its water is replaced on average in less than three years, compared with nearly two centuries in Superior.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Lake Ontario's surface sits roughly a hundred metres lower than Lake Erie's. The connecting Niagara River loses much of that height at Niagara Falls.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Ontario averages about 86 metres deep. That average depth alone is greater than the maximum depth of neighbouring Lake Erie.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Lake Ontario is the last of the five Great Lakes on the journey to the Atlantic. Its outlet becomes the St Lawrence River.
options.label: apps.glerl.noaa.gov

options.text: Ontario has the smallest surface area of the five Great Lakes, yet holds more than three times as much water as Erie. The difference is hidden in its deep basin.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Two volcanoes rise out of the lake to make Ometepe. Concepción and Maderas form the two ends of an island linked by a narrow waist.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Off Granada, the lake breaks into a maze of hundreds of small islands. Their origin lies with Mombacho, the volcano looming above the western shore.
options.label: mapanicaragua.com

options.text: Zapatera is both a lake island and part of a national park. The park includes the smaller islands around it, protecting an archipelago inside Nicaragua's largest lake.
options.label: mined.gob.ni

options.text: Central America's largest lake lies much closer to the Pacific than to the Caribbean, yet drains east. Its outlet is the San Juan River, which carries the water to the Caribbean coast.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: Along the south shore, sand dunes rise as high as 30 metres. This moving sand supports rare plants, some of which grow nowhere outside the Athabasca dunes.
options.label: Source

options.text: Some channels near Lake Athabasca change direction. When an ice jam or flood raises the Peace River above the lake, water runs back toward the lake through the delta.
options.label: Government of Canada

options.text: Two piles of chimney stones and a cellar pit mark the first Fort Chipewyan. The trading post was built in 1788 on a rocky point across the lake from the present community.
options.label: Source

options.text: At the west end of Lake Athabasca is one of the world's largest inland freshwater deltas. The Peace and Athabasca river systems meet in a shifting landscape of lakes and channels.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The world’s largest lake entirely on an island sits on Baffin Island. You have to cross salt water to get to Nettilling even though its own water is fresh.
options.label: Source

options.text: Ringed seals are usually associated with sea ice. An inland population has also been recorded here, in fresh water on Baffin Island.
options.label: Source

options.text: Microscopic algae left a record of the sea in this freshwater lake. Scientists used the chemistry of their shells, buried in lake mud, to trace the transition from marine to brackish water.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Arctic Circle cuts right across Nettilling Lake. Fresh water from this Baffin Island basin drains west through the Koukdjuak River into the shallow tidal waters of Foxe Basin.
options.label: pubs.aina.ucalgary.ca

options.text: Indiana has a Great Lakes shoreline. Its short arc of Lake Michigan lies between the much longer shores of Illinois and Michigan.
options.label: in.gov

options.text: Lake Michigan holds almost twelve times as much water as Lake Erie. Two lakes that look broadly comparable on a continental map conceal very different depths.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: At the Indiana Dunes, wind carries sand up from a freshwater shore. A beach beside a lake supplies dunes tall enough to climb like hills.
options.label: in.gov

options.text: Michigan is the only one of the five Great Lakes with every shore in a single country. Canada shares all four of the others with the United States.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Counting its islands, Huron has the longest shoreline of the five Great Lakes. Larger Lake Superior has less shore to follow.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: The Bruce Peninsula nearly walls off Georgian Bay from the main lake. Stand on one shore of the peninsula and you face the bay, then cross to the other side and you still face Lake Huron.
options.label: epa.gov

options.text: Huron's water is partway through a staircase of lakes. It leaves by the St Clair River, crosses Lake St Clair and continues through the Detroit River to Erie.
options.label: apps.glerl.noaa.gov

options.text: Lake Huron contains the world's largest island in a freshwater lake. Manitoulin Island is itself large enough to hold lakes with islands of their own.
options.label: canada.ca

options.text: Follow the eastern shore by boat and the coast breaks into what locals call the Thirty Thousand Islands. The biosphere reserve follows about 200 kilometres of that shore.
options.label: Source

options.text: Two stone pillars off Flowerpot Island have the outlines of giant plant pots. They gave the island its name and stand above the bay’s clear water.
options.label: Government of Canada

options.text: Some eastern foxsnakes here swim more than ten kilometres. A snake encountered on an outer island can be far from the den where it spent the winter.
options.label: Source

options.text: Georgian Bay looks like a sixth Great Lake, but belongs to Lake Huron. The Bruce Peninsula and Manitoulin Island form much of the barrier between the bay and the main lake.
options.label: publications.gc.ca

options.text: During the siege of Leningrad, trucks crossed Ladoga on a winter ice road. A pipeline and an electric cable also crossed the lake, laid on its bed.
options.label: Source

options.text: Ladoga has its own freshwater ringed seals. Scientists studying when the seals became isolated found an unexpected second line of evidence in the DNA of the lice living on them.
options.label: Source

options.text: On the Valaam archipelago in Lake Ladoga, a monastery rises above the islands. Even the monks’ outer gate has a church built over it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Ladoga is Europe's largest lake. A relatively short river, the Neva, drains this enormous basin through Saint Petersburg into the Baltic.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: The lake floor lies in a rain shadow. The rift floor gets roughly 600 millimetres of rain a year in places, while the surrounding mountains can get about 2,000.
options.label: agl-acare.org

options.text: Two other African Great Lakes feed Albert by different routes. Water from Lake Edward follows the Semliki, while water from Victoria passes through Lake Kyoga.
options.label: agl-acare.org

options.text: Lake Albert fills a long trough on the border of Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The international boundary runs along the lake rather than stopping at its shore.
options.label: wldb.ilec.or.jp

options.text: The Nile barely uses the length of Lake Albert. The Victoria Nile enters near its northern end and the Albert Nile leaves nearby, while the Semliki arrives at the far southern end.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: Along the rocky shore live small, brightly coloured cichlids called mbuna. The lake has produced hundreds of related fish species, many found only here.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: What looks like smoke rising from the water can be a swarm of tiny lake flies. On shore the flies are collected and pressed together to make kungu cakes.
options.label: Source

options.text: A drill lowered into Lake Malawi recovered mud recording 1.3 million years of climate. It showed stretches of extreme drought interrupting periods when the basin overflowed.
options.label: Source

options.text: One long rift lake has three names on the map. Malawi calls it Lake Malawi, Mozambique uses Niassa, and on the Tanzanian shore it is Nyasa.
options.label: ramsar.org

options.text: Thunderstorms here often grow over open water after dark. Night breezes blow from the cooling shores toward each other and lift moist air above the lake.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Lake Victoria produced roughly 500 species of cichlid in about 15,000 years. Mixing between two older fish lineages gave their descendants a head start in genetic variety.
options.label: Source

options.text: Around 15,000 years ago, this vast lake dried out. Mud cores from widely separated parts of the basin preserve the evidence of the dry interval.
options.label: Source

options.text: Victoria is Africa's largest lake by surface area, yet nearby Tanganyika holds much more water. Victoria spreads across a broad, comparatively shallow basin between branches of the East African Rift.
options.label: nilebasin.org

options.text: Vänern has salmon that spend their lives in fresh water. The lake preserves lineages stranded inland as the landscape changed after the last ice age.
options.label: Source

options.text: Ships from the sea can climb all the way to Vänern. Six locks on the route from Gothenburg lift them up to the lake.
options.label: Source

options.text: Sailing the Vänern archipelago takes you past more than bare rock. Some stretches of shore have drifting sand dunes, others wet meadows and fields of wave-worn stones.
options.label: Source

options.text: Vänern is Sweden's largest lake and Europe's third-largest by surface area. Both European lakes ahead of it, Ladoga and Onega, are in Russia.
options.label: smhi.se

options.text: Off Kilwa Island, parts of Mweru are only about two metres deep. A relatively narrow trough holds the deepest water in the lake.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: The number of fish species recorded in Mweru exceeds a hundred. A much smaller subset supplies its commercial fisheries.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: Mweru and Mweru Wantipa are separate lakes near each other. The international border runs through Mweru, while its smaller namesake lies inside Zambia.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: Although it sits close to the lakes of the East African Rift, Mweru sends its water west towards the Atlantic. Its outlet, the Luvua, joins the Lualaba and the Congo.
options.label: fao.org

options.text: Most of the time, this long blue shape on a map of South Australia is a dry salt flat. Thunderstorms sometimes leave shallow patches of water on it.
options.label: National Parks and Wildlife Service South Australia

options.text: When rain filled Lake Torrens in 1989, banded stilts bred there. It was the first documented breeding of the species in South Australia since 1930.
options.label: Source

options.text: When Kokatha applicants sought heritage protection for Lake Torrens, they described the whole lake surface, islands included, as significant under Aboriginal tradition.
options.label: Source

options.text: Rain that reaches Lake Torrens usually has no river route to the sea. The water collects in a closed basin and leaves mainly by evaporation or seepage.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Issyk-Kul tastes slightly salty even though mountain streams feed it. Measurements put it at roughly six grams of salt per litre, well below ocean salinity.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: The basin drops more than six hundred metres below the lake surface. Snow peaks surround a body of water deeper than some seas.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: Wintering waterbirds gather at Issyk-Kul high in the Tian Shan. Open water here provides a stopping place surrounded by frozen mountain country.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: Issyk-Kul sits more than 1,600 metres above the sea, ringed by the Tian Shan. The rivers flowing down from those snowy peaks enter a basin with no surface outlet.
options.label: unesco.org

options.text: The bridges on euro banknotes were imaginary when the notes were designed. Each represents an era of European architecture without giving one country’s landmark pride of place.
options.label: Source

options.text: The EU flag kept its twelve stars as countries joined. The circle represents unity, so you cannot count the member countries by counting the stars.
options.label: Source

options.text: The 1985 Schengen Agreement was signed on a riverboat on the Moselle. The village that gave open borders their name sits where Luxembourg, France and Germany meet.
options.label: Source

options.text: You can cross a land border from Brazil into the European Union. On the far bank of the Oyapock River is French Guiana, an EU region on the South American mainland.
options.label: cp-rup.com

options.text: The name Micronesia means “small islands”, but the islands come in very different heights. Volcanic high islands and low coral atolls share the regional name.
options.label: naturalhistory2.si.edu

options.text: Guam and the Marshall Islands lie in the same geographic region. Between them stretch the Caroline Islands, a reminder that Micronesia covers several separate chains.
options.label: naturalhistory2.si.edu

options.text: Banaba is an unusual Micronesian island. In a country otherwise made up of low atolls, this raised coral island carries an elevated plateau.
options.label: mfed.gov.ki

options.text: Micronesia's islands are scattered across an expanse comparable to Australia, but their combined land area is smaller than Rhode Island. Most of what the regional name covers is ocean.
options.label: naturalhistory2.si.edu

options.text: In Slovenia’s Kras region, the Reka River dives underground. Inside the Škocjan Caves it runs through a canyon whose roof in places is about 150 metres above the water.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: During carnival around Kastav in Croatia, groups in sheepskins walk from village to village with bells tied around their waists. The procession makes its own soundtrack as it moves.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Lake Ohrid, on the Albanian–North Macedonian border, drillers recovered hundreds of metres of lake mud. The record reaches back about 1.36 million years to when a permanent lake formed.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Balkans are easiest to outline from the sea. The Adriatic, Ionian, Aegean and Black seas mark the peninsula on three sides, while its northern edge runs across land.
options.label: cmes.arizona.edu

options.text: In 1976 Mau Piailug guided the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti. He followed the rising points of stars, the sun, moon and ocean swells across the equator.
options.label: Source

options.text: The ancestors of Māori carried kūmara to Aotearoa on their ocean voyages. Centuries later, archaeologists could still identify the crop from microscopic starch grains in old storage pits.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Rapa Nui, carvers shaped most moai from relatively soft volcanic tuff. The picks they used were themselves volcanic rock, made of much harder basalt.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Three islands mark the corners of the Polynesian Triangle. Join Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa New Zealand on a Pacific map and much of Polynesia lies inside.
options.label: nzhistory.govt.nz

options.text: In Vanuatu, a sand artist can draw a whole symmetrical design with one finger in a continuous line. The guiding grid can exist entirely in the artist’s mind.

options.text: Tuvalu's nine islands show three different arrangements of water. Six have lagoons open to the ocean, two have enclosed lagoons, and Niulakita has none.
